description: References supporting technique definitions. Add only sources that have been checked and accurately represented.

references.title: SemEval-2020 Task 11: Detection of Propaganda Techniques in News Articles
references.notes: A shared-task taxonomy and annotated dataset covering techniques including loaded language, repetition, exaggeration or minimisation, doubt, appeal to fear or prejudice, causal oversimplification, slogans, authority appeals and false dilemmas.

references.title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Propaganda in News Articles
references.notes: Research on identifying and explaining propaganda techniques at passage level in news articles.

references.title: Multilingual Multifaceted Understanding of Online News
references.notes: A taxonomy for online news including loaded language, obfuscation or intentional vagueness, exaggeration or minimisation and repetition.

references.title: Rethinking news framing with large language models
references.notes: Experimental research on how selective presentation and tone in otherwise accurate news can shift readers' views and emotional responses.

references.title: Manipulative use of political headlines in western and Russian online sources
references.notes: Study of headline/article discrepancies, expressive language, selective citation and distortions in online political reporting.

references.title: Do Morphemes Matter when Reading Compound Words with Transposed Letters? Evidence from Eye-Tracking and Event-Related Potentials
references.notes: Eye-tracking experiment found longer reading times for misspelled compared with correctly spelled compound words. This supports a reading-disruption mechanism, not deliberate persuasive use.

references.title: One page of text: Eye movements during regular and thorough reading, skimming, and spell checking
references.notes: Eye-tracking research shows how attending to spelling changes reading patterns and can reduce comprehension relative to normal reading. Does not test intentionally planted errors.

references.title: Distinctiveness effect
references.notes: Defines the distinctiveness or von Restorff effect: isolated items can be better remembered. Does not establish that arbitrary misspellings cause persuasion.
